report:
## Yes — the evidence supports this conclusion

Multiple large randomized controlled trials in heavy (current or former) smokers demonstrate that annual or periodic low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduces lung cancer mortality compared with no screening or chest X-ray.

**Key evidence:**

- **NLST (National Lung Screening Trial, US):** In over 53,000 heavy smokers/former smokers aged 55–74, annual LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% compared with chest X-ray screening, along with a 7% reduction in all-cause mortality ([cancer.gov](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst); [atsjournals.org](https://www.atsjournals.org/doi/full/10.1164/rccm.201705-0914OC?cookieSet=1)).

- **NELSON trial (Netherlands/Belgium):** Among ~15,800 heavy smokers randomized to volume-based LDCT at increasing intervals versus no screening, lung-cancer mortality was 24% lower in screened men and 33% lower in screened women, with the trial estimating roughly 60 lung cancer deaths prevented ([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793?cookieSet=1); [mdedge.com](https://www.mdedge.com/familymedicine/article/216378/lung-cancer/rct-confirms-ct-scan-screening-catches-lung-cancer-early)).

- Consistent with these findings, a synthesis of trial evidence concludes: "Systematic lung cancer screening with low-dose CT lowers mortality from lung cancer in (current or former) heavy smokers" ([di.aerzteblatt.de](https://di.aerzteblatt.de/int/archive/article/231736)).

**Caveats:** This mortality benefit comes with tradeoffs—high rates of false-positive findings requiring follow-up procedures, and overdiagnosis (detection of indolent cancers that would not have caused harm), as noted in the same source and corroborated by systematic reviews of screening harms ([di.aerzteblatt.de](https://di.aerzteblatt.de/int/archive/article/231736)).

**Conclusion:** Across two major independent randomized trials (NLST and NELSON), LDCT screening in heavy smokers consistently and significantly reduced lung cancer mortality, confirming the "yes" answer, though clinicians must weigh this against real harms like false positives and overdiagnosis.
